sentences.text: This dinosaur reached a total length of 20 meters and stood 5 meters tall, making it large among dinosaurs but only medium-sized for sauropods.
The holotype specimen includes most of the postcranial skeleton, featuring two well-preserved teeth with wrinkled enamel surfaces.
Twelve chevrons are preserved in the tail region, covering nearly the entire length of the caudal vertebral series.
The species Huabeisaurus allocotus was first described by Pang Qiqing and Cheng Zhengwu in the year 2000.
Numerous remains found during the 1990s include teeth, partial limbs, and vertebrae.
Fossils were discovered at Kangdailiang and Houyu in Zhaojiagou Town, Tianzhen County, Shanxi province, China.
The holotype originally contained 32 caudal vertebrae before some were lost during fossilization or collection.
The holotype was found in the upper member of the Huiquanpu Formation, dated to the Late Cretaceous using ostracods, charophytes, and fission-track dating.
One tooth was found in the quarry, while a second was discovered during field sample preparation at Shijiazhuang University.
The absence of sutures on the vertebrae suggests the specimen was nearing sexual maturity, while open sutures on the scapula and ilium suggest it had not reached full maturity.
D'Emic et al. identified unique features such as divided vertebral laminae, specific caudal rib patterns, a coracoid with a tubercle, and a high tibia-to-femur ratio.
The geological horizon containing an isolated humerus also yielded hadrosaurid specimens and indeterminate ankylosaurid material.
The discoverers erected the family Huabeisauridae for the genus, though this name is not widely used by paleontologists.
Researchers erected the family Huabeisauridae to include Huabeisaurus and the closely related Tangvayosaurus, but Huabeisaurus is classified within the family Saltasauridae.
Huabeisaurus belongs to the parent group Euhelopodidae.
Huabeisaurus was a sauropod dinosaur that lived in northern China during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 99.7 to 70.6 million years ago.
Huabeisaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 72 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now Asia.
It remains uncertain how long the endemism of East Asian sauropods, including Huabeisaurus, lasted.
Pang and Cheng tentatively suggested that Titanosaurus falloti belongs to Huabeisaurus, but this is disputed because the femur lacks uniquely shared features.
